system.name: Try
system.one_liner: a tool that runs an opaque component inside a semisolate to observe, filter, stack and later commit or discard its filesystem effects

components.name: p1
components.role: a process wrapped by try with network access elided and a path masked

components.name: p2
components.role: a process wrapped by try without masking, whose effects are persisted to a named semisolate

components.name: p3
components.role: a process wrapped by try while stacking the effects of the semisolate created for p2

components.name: upperdir
components.role: overlay layer that captures a wrapped process's writes, reads-of-writes, and deletes (as mask files)

components.name: lowerdir
components.role: overlay layer through which reads of untouched paths are served, from the host filesystem or a stacked semisolate

components.name: semisolate
components.role: a named, persisted capture of a process's effects that can later be stacked or committed

components.name: host filesystem
components.role: the real underlying filesystem holding paths alpha, beta, pi and delta

content.key_idea: A worked walkthrough of four try invocations shows how each one captures a wrapped process's filesystem effects in an overlay upperdir, how effects can be filtered, persisted as a named semisolate, or stacked onto a later invocation, and how a final commit applies stacked effects back onto the real host filesystem from bottom to top.
content.reading_order: Left to right across four try invocations (p1, p2, p3, and p3's commit), each read top to bottom through its invocation command, captured component effects, internal upperdir/lowerdir state, and resulting host filesystem state.

summary: Try wraps an opaque component so its filesystem effects can be observed, filtered, stacked and later committed or discarded. Figure 2 is a matrix walkthrough of four try invocations, one per column, each read top to bottom through its invocation command, the component effects it captures, its internal upperdir/lowerdir overlay state, and the resulting host filesystem state. The first invocation elides network access and masks a path; the second persists its effects as a named semisolate after excluding one write; the third stacks the second's semisolate as its lowerdir and captures further effects; the fourth (grayed out) shows committing the stacked semisolate's effects onto the real filesystem from bottom to top. The figure is a dense, code-like diagram with monospace command headers, rounded gray overlay boxes, small lock icons for masked paths, and many thin arrows linking commands to effects to filesystem state.
